An excrescence is an ugly, abnormal outgrowth — something that has grown or been added onto something else in a way that is unwanted, out of place, and makes the whole thing worse. Think of it as an "ugly extra bit that doesn't belong." It can refer to something physical, or it can be used more broadly as powerful criticism of anything — a building, a piece of writing, a law, a social institution — that has had something unnecessary and ugly grafted onto it.

In its most concrete sense, an excrescence is an abnormal growth on a living body. A wart, a cyst, a polyp, a tumour — anything that protrudes outward from a surface where it has no business being. It is not just any growth; it is specifically one that is disfiguring, irregular, and unwanted.

The word can also apply to non-living surfaces. An ugly, awkward bulge or protrusion on a wall, a rock formation, or a piece of furniture can be called an excrescence, as long as it juts out in a way that looks wrong and spoils the appearance of the whole.

"The surgeon removed a small excrescence from the patient's wrist."
"Years of water damage had left a lumpy excrescence on the plaster wall."
The Figurative Meaning — Where the Word Really Shines

This is where excrescence becomes a genuinely powerful and expressive word. Used figuratively, it describes any unnecessary, ugly addition to a system, institution, text, piece of art, or idea — something that has attached itself like a growth, serving no purpose and making the original thing worse.

Picture a clean, elegant novel that suddenly has a chapter crammed in that goes nowhere, adds nothing, and disrupts the entire rhythm of the book. That chapter is an excrescence. Or imagine a well-designed building that has had an ugly glass box stuck onto its side by a later owner — that addition is an excrescence. Or think of a simple, fair law that has had so many clumsy amendments piled onto it over the decades that it has become bloated and incoherent — those amendments are excrescences.

"Critics called the new stadium an architectural excrescence that completely destroyed the beauty of the historic waterfront."
"The final act of the play was a dramatic excrescence — it undid everything the first two acts had carefully built."
"What began as a straightforward tax code became, over the years, a monstrous excrescence of loopholes and contradictions."

The figurative use always carries these ideas together:

  • It doesn't belong there
  • It has "grown" onto something that was originally fine
  • It actively disfigures or degrades the whole
  • It ought to be cut away
The Emotional Weight of the Word

This is crucial: excrescence is never a neutral word. It is a word of strong disapproval and, often, disgust. When you call something an excrescence, you are not merely saying it is "unnecessary" or "extra." You are saying it is ugly, wrong, and almost offensive — like a disfigurement. The comparison to a physical growth (a wart, a tumour) is entirely intentional; the word carries that sense of something diseased and unnatural having attached itself where it should not be.

If someone says a policy is "redundant," that is mild criticism. If they call it an excrescence, that is a sharp, contemptuous dismissal. The word is a scalpel — precise and cutting.

In the study of language, excrescence has a specific technical meaning: the development of an extra sound within a word that wasn't originally there, usually slipping in uninvited to make the word easier to pronounce.

The classic example is the letter "p" in the word "empty." The word originally had no "p" — it came from an older form closer to "emty." But over time, speakers naturally inserted a "p" between the "m" and the "t" sounds (try saying "emty" quickly — your lips almost force a "p" in there). That intruder "p" is a linguistic excrescence. Similarly, many people naturally say a faint "p" sound in "warmth" (making it sound like "wormpth") — again, an excrescence.

The logic is exactly the same as the main meaning: a sound that does not belong, that crept in uninvited, and attached itself to something it was never part of.

At the heart of every use of excrescence — whether physical, figurative, or linguistic — is one consistent image: something has grown where it has no right to grow, disfiguring the thing it has attached itself to. It is always unwanted. It is always ugly. And the strong implication is always that things would be better if it were removed.

Use this word when you want to say that something is not just unnecessary, but actively wrong and disfiguring — a blemish on something that could otherwise be clean, beautiful, or good.
